resources.title: What to Expect at Prenatal Visits
resources.summary: Learn about routine checkups and what happens at each trimester
resources.content:
Prenatal care is designed to improve the health and well-being of pregnant individuals and their children. Regular prenatal visits are essential for monitoring your health and your baby's development.

**When should you book your first prenatal visit?**
It is best to schedule your first prenatal appointment as soon as you get a positive pregnancy test and time it ideally around the 7-10 week mark in pregnancy for the first visit.

**First Trimester Visit (Weeks 1-12)**
A comprehensive prenatal visit is typically recommended before 10 weeks of pregnancy. This appointment often includes a review of your medical history and routine prenatal lab tests such as a complete blood count, blood type and Rh(D) status, antibody screening, urinalysis, diabetes screening, immunity testing, and STI screening. Beginning at 10 weeks, optional aneuploidy screening may be offered to assess for certain chromosomal conditions. More information about noninvasive prenatal testing can be found [here](https://www.cdph.ca.gov/Programs/CFH/DGDS/pages/pns/default.aspx). Your provider may also discuss mental health, substance use, nutrition, exercise, medications, breastfeeding, and preparation for birth. An early ultrasound may be performed to confirm the pregnancy, detect a heartbeat, and establish an estimated due date.

**Second Trimester Visits (Weeks 13-27)**
Prenatal visits during the second trimester typically occur every 4 weeks. Around 20 weeks, most patients receive an anatomy ultrasound to evaluate the baby's growth and development, examine major organs, and assess the placenta and amniotic fluid. Many parents also choose to learn the baby's sex during this scan. More information about the anatomy scan can be found [here](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/22644-20-week-ultrasound). Between 24 and 28 weeks, screening for gestational diabetes is typically performed with a glucose tolerance test (GTT). During this trimester, your provider may also discuss signs of preterm labor, postpartum planning, and choosing a healthcare provider for your baby.

**Third Trimester Visits (Weeks 28-40)**
Visits become more frequent, around every 2 weeks until 36 weeks, then weekly. Your provider will monitor fetal movement and positioning, check for signs of labor, and screen for signs and symptoms of preeclampsia. You may also receive repeat STI testing, as well as additional immunizations or injections, such as Rh(D), seasonal RSV, and Tdap. Between weeks 36 and 37, GBS screening will take place, a routine test for Group B Streptococcus bacteria. This bacterium can cause severe infections in newborns. A positive test means that you carry the bacteria and may need IV antibiotics during labor. More information about GBS testing can be found [here](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/group-b-strep).

**What should you bring to your appointments?**
- List of questions
- Current medications
- Insurance card
- Support person if desired

To see a sample schedule for prenatal care visits, please visit the [ACOG sample prenatal care schedule](https://cdn-links.lww.com/permalink/aog/e/aog_145_5_2025_03_28_jones_25-345_sdc5.pdf).

**Sources:**
- [ACOG: Sample Prenatal Care Schedule](https://cdn-links.lww.com/permalink/aog/e/aog_145_5_2025_03_28_jones_25-345_sdc5.pdf)
- [ACOG: Prevention of Group B Streptococcal Early-Onset Disease in Newborns](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2020/02/prevention-of-group-b-streptococcal-early-onset-disease-in-newborns)
- [ACOG: Tailored Prenatal Care Delivery for Pregnant Individuals](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/clinical-consensus/articles/2025/04/tailored-prenatal-care-delivery-for-pregnant-individuals)
- [ACOG: Screening for Fetal Chromosomal Abnormalities](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/practice-advisory/articles/2026/01/screening-for-fetal-chromosomal-abnormalities)

resources.title: Nutrition During Pregnancy
resources.summary: Guidelines for nutrition during pregnancy to support your baby's growth and development

image.alt: Fresh healthy vegetables and fruits for pregnancy nutrition

resources.content:
Guidelines for nutrition during pregnancy to support your baby's growth and development.

**Important nutrients:**
- **Folic Acid**: 600 mcg daily. Folic acid supports fetal growth and development and helps prevent serious birth defects of the brain and spine known as neural tube defects. Good dietary sources include dark green leafy vegetables, fortified cereals, and enriched breads and pastas. In addition to a folate-rich diet, taking a daily prenatal vitamin containing 400 mcg of folic acid is recommended.
- **Iron**: 27 mg daily. Pregnant women need additional iron to help red blood cells deliver oxygen to the fetus. Iron can be supplemented, or found in foods such as lean red meat, poultry, fish, beans, and iron-fortified cereals.
- **Calcium**: 1,000 - 1,300 mg depending on age. Calcium is needed to build strong bones and teeth for your fetus. Good sources of calcium include milk, cheese, yogurt, sardines, and dark green leafy vegetables.
- **Iodine**: 220 mcg. Needed for healthy brain development of fetus. Dietary sources include iodized salt, dairy products, seafood, meat, and eggs.
- **Choline**: 450 mg. Important for the development of the fetus's brain and spinal cord. Sources of choline include milk, eggs, peanuts, and soy products.
- **Omega-3 Fatty Acids**: These fats are important for the development of your fetus's brain. Dietary sources of omega-3s include fish and shellfish, flaxseed, broccoli, cantaloupe, kidney beans, spinach, and walnuts.
- Other important vitamins include Vitamins A, C, D, B6, and B12

**Foods to avoid:**
- Raw or undercooked fish, meat, or eggs
- High mercury fish (bigeye tuna, king mackerel, marlin, shark, or swordfish). Limit white albacore tuna to only 6 oz a week.
- Unpasteurized (raw) milk or cheeses
- Deli meats and hot dogs should be cooked thoroughly to kill any bacteria
- Alcohol

For more information, please visit [ACOG: Healthy Eating During Pregnancy](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/healthy-eating-during-pregnancy).

**Sources:**
- [ACOG: Healthy Eating During Pregnancy](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/healthy-eating-during-pregnancy)
- [ACOG: The Top 6 Pregnancy Questions I Hear From First-Time Moms](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/experts-and-stories/the-latest/the-top-6-pregnancy-questions-i-hear-from-first-time-moms)
- [CDC: Folic Acid Intake and Sources](https://www.cdc.gov/folic-acid/about/intake-and-sources.html)
- [WHO: Daily Iron Supplementation in Pregnancy](https://www.who.int/tools/elena/interventions/daily-iron-pregnancy)

resources.title: When to Call Your Provider
resources.summary: Warning signs that need immediate attention
resources.content:
Some symptoms during pregnancy require prompt medical attention. Trust your instincts - you know your body best.

**Call immediately for:**
- Vaginal bleeding or fluid leaking
- Severe abdominal pain
- Severe headache that doesn't go away
- Dizziness or fainting
- Trouble breathing
- Chest pain
- Vision changes
- Extreme swelling of face or hands
- Severe swelling, redness or pain of your leg or arm
- Decreased fetal movement
- Signs of labor before 37 weeks
- Fever of 100.4°F or higher
- Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby

**Contact your provider for:**
- Persistent nausea/vomiting
- Painful urination
- Unusual vaginal discharge
- Concerns about baby's movement

**UCI Labor & Delivery:** (949) 824-8200
**Emergency:** Call 911

**Sources:**
- [CDC: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs](https://www.cdc.gov/hearher/maternal-warning-signs/index.html)
- [ACOG: Quality and Safety Resources](https://www.acog.org/giving/programs/quality-and-safety/resources)

resources.title: Understanding Your Pregnancy
resources.summary: Changes you may notice and how your baby grows in each trimester
resources.content:
Pregnancy is a time of significant changes as your body grows and prepares to welcome your baby. Every pregnancy is unique, and your experience may be different from someone else's. This guide is meant to provide a general understanding of changes you may notice, how your baby is growing, and when to reach out to your care team.

**First trimester (Weeks 1-13)**
During the first trimester, your baby begins developing major organs and body systems. You may experience fatigue, nausea or vomiting, breast tenderness, increased urination, bloating, and mood changes. Some people have few symptoms, while others experience more significant discomfort.

**How your baby grows in weeks 1-8:**
- The brain and spine begin to form
- Cardiac tissue starts to develop
- Muscles of the eyes, nose, and mouth form
- Webbed fingers and toes poke out from developing hands and feet
- The lungs start to form the tubes that will carry air in and out after birth
- The inner ear begins to develop

**How your baby grows in weeks 9-12:**
- Cartilage for the limbs, hands, and feet start to form but won't harden into bones for a few weeks
- Eyelids form but remain closed
- Genitals begin to form
- Liver begins development
- Kidneys begin making urine
- Pancreas starts making insulin
- Fingernails form

**Second trimester (Weeks 14-27)**
Many people find that nausea and fatigue improve during the second trimester. You may notice a growing belly, increased appetite, skin changes, constipation, heartburn, and back or pelvic discomfort. You may begin feeling your baby move, often between 16 and 22 weeks.

**How your baby grows in weeks 13-16:**
- Bones harden, especially the long bones
- Skin is thin and see-through but will start to thicken soon
- Toenails form
- Neck is defined and lower limbs are developed
- Hearing starts to develop
- Lungs begin to form tissue that will allow them to exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide when breathing starts after birth

**How your baby grows in weeks 17-20:**
- The part of the brain that controls motor movements is fully formed
- Digestive system is working
- Ears, nose, and lips are recognizable on an ultrasound exam
- In girls, the uterus and vagina are starting to form
- Soft, downy hair called lanugo starts to form and cover the body

**How your baby grows in weeks 21-24:**
- Kicks and turns are stronger
- Sucking reflex is developing
- Fat is forming under the skin
- Ridges form in the hands and feet that later will be fingerprints and footprints
- Skin is wrinkled and reddish from visible blood vessels

**How your baby grows in weeks 25-28:**
- Lungs are fully formed but not yet ready to function outside the uterus
- Loud sounds can make your fetus respond with a startled movement and pull in the arms and legs
- Eyelids can open and close
- Lungs begin to make surfactant, a substance needed for breathing after birth
- Nervous system is developing
- Skin begins to look smoother as more fat is added

**Third trimester (Weeks 28-40+)**
As your baby continues to grow, you may experience increased pressure on your bladder, shortness of breath, heartburn, difficulty sleeping, swelling in your feet and ankles, and Braxton Hicks contractions. You may also notice changes in your baby's movement patterns.

**How your baby grows in weeks 29-32:**
- The fetus can stretch, kick, and make grasping motions
- Eyes can sense changes in light
- Bone marrow is forming red blood cells
- Head may have some hair
- In boys, the testicles have begun to descend into the scrotum
- Lanugo begins to disappear

**How your baby grows in weeks 33-36:**
- Bones harden but the skull remains soft and flexible
- Fingernails have grown to the end of the fingers
- Limbs begin to look chubby
- The fetus may turn into a head-down position for birth

**How your baby grows in weeks 37-40:**
- Circulatory system is done developing
- Musculoskeletal system also is done developing
- Lungs, brain, and nervous system are finishing their development
- Fat continues to be added all over to keep the baby warm after birth

**Common pregnancy symptoms:**
- Nausea and vomiting
- Fatigue
- Breast tenderness
- Frequent urination
- Constipation and bloating
- Heartburn
- Back pain
- Leg cramps
- Mild swelling of the feet and ankles
- Mood changes

If you are unsure whether a symptom is normal, contact your prenatal care team.

**When to seek medical care**
Call your UCI Health prenatal care team or Labor & Delivery if you experience:
- Vaginal bleeding, especially heavy bleeding
- Leaking fluid from the vagina
- Regular painful contractions or signs of preterm labor
- Decreased or absent fetal movement after you have started feeling your baby move
- Severe abdominal pain or persistent vomiting
- Severe headache, vision changes, sudden swelling of the face or hands, or pain in the upper abdomen
- Fever, difficulty breathing, chest pain, or fainting

Call 911 for severe difficulty breathing, chest pain, loss of consciousness, or other life-threatening symptoms.

If you are concerned about your health or your baby's health, do not wait for your next appointment. Your care team can help you decide what to do.

**Sources:**
- [ACOG: How Your Fetus Grows During Pregnancy](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/how-your-fetus-grows-during-pregnancy)

resources.title: Planning Ahead for Postpartum
resources.summary: What to arrange for you and your baby before delivery
resources.content:
The weeks after delivery are an important time for you and your baby to rest, recover, and adjust to life together. Before your baby arrives, take time to prepare for your postpartum care and newborn needs.

**Before delivery:**
- Choose a pediatrician and schedule newborn appointment; if choosing UCI pediatrics, we will help make the baby's appointment when you are at the hospital
- Discuss breastfeeding, formula feeding, or combination feeding
- Make a plan for postpartum contraception and future pregnancy spacing
- Arrange support at home, including transportation and help with meals, childcare, and daily activities
- Prepare newborn supplies and a safe sleep space
- Learn about postpartum recovery, mental health, and warning signs

**After delivery:**
- Schedule your postpartum follow-up with your UCI Health care team
- Reach out to your care team if you have concerns about your recovery, feeding, mood, or your baby's health
- Consider immunization with the MMR vaccine (if you are not already immune) or the HPV vaccine (if you are not already vaccinated)

resources.title: Giving Birth at a Teaching Hospital
resources.summary: What to expect at UCI Medical Center and who may be in the room
resources.content:
UCI Medical Center is an academic teaching hospital. That means your care team includes physicians and nurses who are completing their training, working alongside and supervised by experienced, board-certified providers and registered nurses. It's a normal part of how academic medical centers work, and it usually means more people watching over you and your baby. If you would prefer not to have resident physicians or trainees participating in your care, you have the right to seek care at a non-teaching facility.

**Who you may meet on your care team:**
- **Your labor and delivery nurse**: your main bedside caregiver. They monitor you and your baby, coordinate your care, and are your go-to person for questions, comfort, and advocacy.
- **Attending physician**: a board-certified OB/GYN or Family Medicine doctor who oversees all care decisions and holds final responsibility for your delivery.
- **Residents**: fully licensed physicians who have finished medical school and are completing specialty training. They help manage your labor and may assist with or perform your delivery under attending supervision.
- **Fellows (in some cases)**: physicians who finished residency and are training further in a subspecialty such as maternal-fetal medicine. You may meet one if your pregnancy is high-risk.
- **Medical students**: students in their clinical rotations. They observe, help with basic tasks, and may ask about your medical history.
- **Nursing students**: student nurses gaining hands-on experience, working alongside your assigned nurse.
- **Anesthesia team**: if you choose an epidural, an anesthesiologist or certified nurse anesthetist places and manages it. An anesthesia resident or fellow may be involved, supervised by an attending anesthesiologist.
- **Others who may join**: a pediatric or neonatal team for your baby after birth, a lactation consultant, a social worker

**Why a teaching hospital can be a good thing:**
- More trained eyes on you and your baby throughout labor
- Academic centers are closely connected to current, evidence-based practice
- Trainees are often especially thorough and attentive
- A full range of specialists is available on site if something unexpected comes up, including anesthesia, maternal-fetal medicine, and a neonatal intensive care team
- Care is delivered by a team and a physician is always at the hospital and available, day or night

**We want to empower you to:**
- Know who is in your room, their name, and their role
- Ask anyone to introduce themselves and explain what they're doing and why
- Ask for the room to be cleared of anyone whose presence isn't necessary
- Bring your support person or doula, within unit visitor guidelines
- Welcome trainees. Many patients find the extra attention and support genuinely helpful, and some enjoy being part of training the next generation of clinicians.

**How to make your preferences known:**
- Tell your nurse your comfort level as soon as you're admitted, so it can be shared with the whole team
- Write your preferences about trainees into your birth plan and bring a copy

**Helpful things to say:**
- "I'd prefer only essential staff in the room for the delivery."
- "I'm okay with students observing, but I'd rather my exams be done by my nurse or the resident physician."
- "I've changed my mind. I'd like fewer people in the room now."

If you ever feel unheard, uncomfortable, or unsure who someone is, start with your labor nurse. You can also ask for the charge nurse or the attending physician. UCI Health also has patient advocacy services available to help you resolve concerns during your stay.

resources.title: Signs of Labor
resources.summary: How to know when labor is starting
resources.content:
Recognizing the signs of labor helps you know when it's time to head to the hospital. For low-risk pregnancies, it is advised to labor at home until active labor begins.

**Early signs (days to hours before):**
- "Nesting" urge (burst of energy)
- Loose stools
- Backache
- Lightening (baby drops lower)
- Highly irregular contractions (contractions come and go randomly, vary in duration)
- "Bloody show": loss of mucus plug, passage of blood-stained mucus, early sign of cervical changes

**True labor signs:**
- Regular, painful uterine contractions that get closer together and more intense. This is the most reliable indicator (you can use the 5-1-1 rule: 5 minutes apart, for 1 minute each, for 1 hour)
- Contractions that don't stop with rest or hydration, which differentiates them from Braxton Hicks
- Water breaking (may be a gush or trickle)
- 6 cm dilation of cervix. If you have given birth before, you may want to come in before this cutoff since labor may progress faster

**[5-1-1 Rule](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/how-to-tell-when-labor-begins) for first-time moms (from ACOG):**
Call or come in when contractions are:
- **5** minutes apart
- Lasting **1** minute each
- For **1** hour

**Come to the hospital immediately, regardless of contraction timing, for any of the following:**
- Water breaking
- Vaginal bleeding beyond bloody show
- Significantly decreased or absent movement of baby
- Severe and constant abdominal pain

**Sources:**
- [ACOG: How to Tell When Labor Begins](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/how-to-tell-when-labor-begins)
- [ACOG Committee Opinion No. 766: Approaches to Limit Intervention During Labor and Birth (2019). Obstetrics & Gynecology, 133(2), e164-e173](https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000003074)

resources.title: Pain Management Options
resources.summary: Understanding your options for comfort during labor
resources.content:
There is no single "right" way to cope with labor pain. What matters most is that you feel supported and in control. Research shows a sense of empowerment and control predicts satisfaction with birth more than which method you choose (Smith 2021; Bryant/ACOG 2019). Many people combine comfort measures and medication. Talk through your preferences with your provider before labor and know you can change your mind at any time.

**Comfort measures**
These are safe options, though how well each one works varies from person to person. We may not have all of these options available at the time you deliver at UCI, so please discuss with your clinician team as well.
- **Continuous labor support**: a partner, nurse, or doula who stays with you. Linked to less use of pain medication.
- **Movement and upright positions**: walking, swaying, hands-and-knees, birth ball. Also linked to less pain medication use.
- **Water**: a warm shower or tub, where available
- **Massage, counter-pressure, and warm packs**: may lower pain intensity and even shorten labor
- **Breathing, relaxation, and visualization**: including yoga, hypnosis, and music therapy
- **TENS unit**: mild electrical pulses on the skin

**Medication options**
- **Epidural and other neuraxial options**: the most effective pain relief method. Used in about 75% of U.S. births (Smith 2021; ACOG Practice Bulletin 209, 2019).
- **Epidural**: a thin, flexible tube (catheter) is placed in your lower back to deliver numbing medicine continuously. It can stay in place all through labor and can be used for a cesarean if one becomes necessary. You can press a button for extra doses when you need them.
- **Spinal**: a single injection with fast relief; no catheter, so it doesn't provide ongoing doses

**Good to know about epidurals:**
- Timing is flexible: you can request one at any point in labor; you don't have to wait for a certain dilation
- You'll likely still feel pressure and the urge to push, but not sharp pain
- The dose can often be adjusted for pushing
- It can help you rest during a long labor
- Epidurals do not increase the chance of cesarean or vacuum-assisted delivery. They lengthen the pushing stage by an average of only about 8 minutes, with no harm to the baby (Kearns 2023).
- Compared with IV opioids, epidurals are linked to less breathing difficulty in newborns (Wilson/RESPITE 2018; Kearns 2023).

**IV or injected opioids:**
- Options include morphine and fentanyl
- They may take the edge off, and no single opioid is clearly better than the rest (Smith 2021)
- Relief is often limited and unpredictable; side effects can include nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, and itching
- Opioids cross the placenta and can temporarily affect the baby's breathing, muscle tone, and feeding, though no long-term effects have been found (Smith LA, Cochrane 2018; Kearns 2023)

**Local anesthesia:**
- Numbing medicine injected into a specific area. For example, for a vaginal tear to be repaired after delivery. It does not relieve contraction pain.

**If you have a history of opioid use disorder:**
- You deserve full, effective pain relief
- Your UCI healthcare team will build an individualized plan with you and your care team during pregnancy, before labor begins

**After birth:**
- For soreness and cramping: ibuprofen (600 mg every 6 hours) and acetaminophen (975 mg every 8 hours, or 650 mg every 6 hours)
- Routine opioids aren't needed after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. Most discomfort is mild to moderate and improves within about two weeks
- For perineal soreness, ice packs, warm packs, and topical numbing or hydrocortisone preparations may help, though the evidence is limited

**Remember:**
- Your plan can change during labor
- Every option, including no medication, is a valid choice
- Wanting pain relief is reason enough
- ACOG states that maternal request is a sufficient medical indication for pain relief during labor (ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 209, 2019)
- Your care team will support whatever you decide

**Sources:**
- Smith A, Laflamme E, Komanecky C. Pain Management in Labor. American Family Physician. 2021;103(6):355-364.
- Bryant AS, Borders AE. Approaches to Limit Intervention During Labor and Birth. American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists; 2019.
- Jones L, Othman M, Dowswell T, et al. Pain Management for Women in Labour: An Overview of Systematic Reviews. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012;(3):CD009234. [doi:10.1002/14651858.CD009234.pub2](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD009234.pub2)
- Smith CA, Levett KM, Collins CT, et al. Massage, Reflexology and Other Manual Methods for Pain Management in Labour. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018;3:CD009290. [doi:10.1002/14651858.CD009290.pub3](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD009290.pub3)
- Zuarez-Easton S, Erez O, Zafran N, et al. Pharmacologic and Nonpharmacologic Options for Pain Relief During Labor: An Expert Review. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2023;228(5S):S1246-S1259. [doi:10.1016/j.ajog.2023.03.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajog.2023.03.003)
- Chang CY, Gau ML, Huang CJ, Cheng HM. Effects of Non-Pharmacological Coping Strategies for Reducing Labor Pain: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis. PLoS One. 2022;17(1):e0261493. [doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0261493](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0261493)
- Ecker J, Abuhamad A, Hill W, et al. Substance Use Disorders in Pregnancy: Clinical, Ethical, and Research Imperatives of the Opioid Epidemic. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2019;221(1):B5-B28. [doi:10.1016/j.ajog.2019.03.022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajog.2019.03.022)
- Pharmacologic Stepwise Multimodal Approach for Postpartum Pain Management: ACOG Clinical Consensus No. 1. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2021;138(3):507-517. [doi:10.1097/AOG.0000000000004517](https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000004517)
- Nanji JA, Carvalho B. Pain Management During Labor and Vaginal Birth. Best Practice & Research Clinical Obstetrics & Gynaecology. 2020;67:100-112. [doi:10.1016/j.bpobgyn.2020.03.002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bpobgyn.2020.03.002)
- Wilson MJA, MacArthur C, Hewitt CA, et al. Intravenous Remifentanil Patient-Controlled Analgesia Versus Intramuscular Pethidine for Pain Relief in Labour (RESPITE). Lancet. 2018;392(10148):662-672. [doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31613-1](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736%2818%2931613-1)

resources.title: What to Pack for the Hospital
resources.summary: Essential items for your hospital stay
resources.content:
Pack your bag by 37 weeks' gestation!

The average hospital stay for childbirth in the United States is approximately 24-48 hours after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and 2-4 days (48-96 hours) after a cesarean delivery, so pack accordingly!

UCI Hospital Orange provides a [Maternity Tour of the Labor and Delivery unit](https://www.ucihealth.org/health-and-wellness/events/health-classes/orange-maternity-tour) for anyone who is interested in learning more about what to expect during your hospital stay.

**For the birthing person:**
- ID and insurance cards
- Copy of Birth Plan (if you have one)
- Clothing for labor: loose and comfortable robe or gown, slip-on shoes
- Toiletries (toothbrush, lip balm, hair ties, lotion, personal hygiene items, etc.)
- Glasses (instead of contacts)
- Shower shoes, sandals/slippers
- Phone and charger
- Comfort items: blanket, pillow, playlist, speaker for music, white noise machine, personal fan
- Re-usable water bottle with a straw. Thirst is very common during labor and using a straw can be easier
- Snacks and drinks

**About eating and drinking during labor:**
- The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) both support oral intake of moderate amounts of liquids for uncomplicated laboring patients, for example water, fruit juices without pulp, carbonated beverages, clear tea, black coffee, and sports drinks
- WHO recommends water, juice, isotonic drinks (for example Gatorade), and light meals or snacks (light carbohydrate diets, high-protein diets)
- Your care team will advise you when to stop eating solid foods, typically once labor is active or if complications arise
- If having an elective/planned cesarean delivery: solid food fasting for 8 hours and clear liquids up to 2 hours before anesthesia

**For after birth:**
- Going-home outfit (nursing bra, comfortable underwear, loose clothing)
- Going-home outfit for baby
- Information of pediatrician if you have a specific person in mind (otherwise UCI will help you get your initial 2-3 day baby visit appointment at UCI)
- Infant car seat (installed in the vehicle, do not need to bring up to the room)

**For your support person:**
- Snacks
- A few changes of clothes; PJs
- Toiletries

**UCI provides:**
- Hospital gown
- Mesh underwear and pads
- Grip socks
- Basic toiletries, witch hazel pads, lanolin cream
- Diapers and wipes
- Baby blanket
- Lactation consultations
- [Maternity education classes](https://www.ucihealth.org/search?searchType=events&event_categories=Health%20Class): Breastfeeding Education, UCI Health - Orange Maternity Tour, Newborn Care, Childbirth Preparation (Four-Week Series)

**Sources:**
- Zhu C, Zhou L, Tang Y. Oral intake management in laboring women: a scoping review. Front Med (Lausanne). 2025;12:1690743. [doi:10.3389/fmed.2025.1690743](https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2025.1690743)
- Practice Guidelines for Obstetric Anesthesia: An Updated Report by the American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Obstetric Anesthesia and the Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology. Anesthesiology. 2016;124(2):270-300. [doi:10.1097/ALN.0000000000000935](https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000000935)
- ACOG Committee Opinion No. 766: Approaches to Limit Intervention During Labor and Birth. Obstetrics & Gynecology. 2019;133(2):e164-e173. [doi:10.1097/AOG.0000000000003074](https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000003074)

categories.title: After Baby Arrives
categories.description: Recovery, newborn care, and adjusting to parenthood

heroImage.alt: Mother bonding with her newborn baby

resources.title: Your Physical Recovery
resources.summary: What to expect in the weeks after birth
resources.content:
Your body needs time to heal after birth. Be patient with yourself. ACOG calls this the "[fourth trimester](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2018/05/optimizing-postpartum-care)" - a critical period for recovery.

**[First few days](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/postpartum-pain-management):**
- Vaginal bleeding (lochia) - normal for 4-6 weeks
- Cramping, especially while breastfeeding
- Soreness in perineum or incision area
- Breast engorgement when milk comes in
- Sweating, especially at night
- Hemorrhoids
- [Bladder and bowel problems](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/pelvic-support-problems)

**Recovery tips:**
- Rest as much as possible
- Accept help from others
- Stay hydrated
- Use ice packs for swelling
- Take medications as prescribed
- Move gently to prevent blood clots
- Refrain from sexual intercourse until first postpartum visit

**After cesarean (c-section):**
- Keep incision clean and dry
- Avoid lifting heavy objects (over 10 lbs) for 6 weeks
- Support your belly when coughing or laughing

**Call your provider if:**
- Fever over 100.4°F
- Heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in 1 hour)
- Severe pain not relieved by medication
- Signs of infection (redness, pus, foul odor)
- Difficulty breathing or chest pain
- Leg pain or swelling (one side)

resources.title: Newborn Care Basics
resources.summary: Essential information for caring for your new baby

image.alt: Father caring for newborn baby - partner support

resources.content:
Caring for a newborn can feel overwhelming, but you'll learn quickly!

**Feeding:**
- Feed on demand, usually every 2-3 hours
- Look for hunger cues: rooting, hand-to-mouth
- 8-12 feedings per day is normal
- Supplement with [400 IU vitamin D per day](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/feeding-nutrition/Pages/Vitamin-Iron-Supplements.aspx), discuss with your baby's doctor

**Diapering:**
- Expect 6-8 wet diapers per day once milk comes in
- Clean umbilical stump with water, keep dry
- Fold diaper below stump until it falls off

**[Safe Sleep](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/a-parents-guide-to-safe-sleep.aspx) (AAP Guidelines):**
- Newborns sleep 16-17+ hours per day in stretches
- **Always place baby on back to sleep** - reduces SIDS risk
- Keep crib free of loose bedding, toys, bumpers
- [Room share (not bed share)](https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/safe-sleep/) for first 6-12 months
- Monitor for overheating (flushed skin, sweating, hot chest) while asleep, reduce by one layer of clothing/blanket and recheck soon

**Bathing:**
- Sponge baths only until cord falls off
- 2-3 baths per week is plenty
- Keep room warm

**Normal newborn things:**
- Sneezing (clearing passages)
- Hiccups
- Irregular breathing patterns
- Startle reflex
- Peeling skin

**[First newborn visit](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/Your-Childs-Checkups/Pages/Your-Checkup-Checklist-Newborn-Visit-2-to-5-days-old.aspx):**
- 48-72 hours after leaving hospital
- Bring hospital paperwork if baby's doctor is outside UCI
- Don't hesitate to call the office before if any questions or concerns

**Learn More:**
- [AAP Safe Sleep Guidelines](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/a-parents-guide-to-safe-sleep.aspx)
- [CDC Safe Sleep for Babies](https://www.cdc.gov/sudden-infant-death/sleep-safely/index.html)

resources.title: Your Postpartum Checkup
resources.summary: What happens at your follow-up appointment
resources.content:
Your postpartum visit is an important check on your recovery.

**When:**
- Initial contact within first 4-6 weeks
- Earlier if you had a cesarean or complications (typically 2 week c-section check)
- May have additional check-ins by phone

**What to expect:**
- Physical exam
- Check incision or perineal healing
- Blood pressure check
- Discussion of birth control options
- [Screening for postpartum depression](https://www.acog.org/programs/perinatal-mental-health/patient-screening)
- Address any concerns or questions

**Topics to discuss:**
- How [you're feeling emotionally](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/postpartum-depression)
- Feeding challenges
- Sleep and fatigue
- Pain or complications
- [Return to exercise](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/exercise-after-pregnancy)
- [Intimacy and birth control](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/using-long-acting-reversible-contraception-right-after-childbirth)
- Support system

**Prepare by:**
- Writing down questions
- Writing down any symptoms or concerns
- Bringing your baby (or arranging childcare)
- Being honest about how you're really feeling

**Learn More:**
- [ACOG: What to Expect at Your Postpartum Checkup](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/experts-and-stories/the-latest/what-to-expect-at-a-postpartum-checkup-and-why-the-visit-matters)
- [ACOG: Postpartum Depression](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/postpartum-depression)
- [ACOG: Exercise After Pregnancy](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/exercise-after-pregnancy)
- [ACOG: Long-Acting Reversible Contraception Right After Childbirth](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/using-long-acting-reversible-contraception-right-after-childbirth)

categories.title: Mental Health & Wellness
categories.description: Emotional wellbeing during pregnancy and postpartum

heroImage.alt: Supportive women's community - peer support for mental health

resources.title: Perinatal Mental Health
resources.summary: Baby blues, depression, anxiety, psychosis, and PTSD during pregnancy and after birth
resources.content:
Perinatal mood and anxiety disorders are some of the most common complications that happen either during pregnancy or in the first 12 months postpartum. Despite the increasing prevalence and negative effects associated with these conditions, perinatal mental health disorders often remain unacknowledged, under-diagnosed and untreated.

**Postpartum Baby Blues**
The baby blues that some people may experience postpartum are a common and temporary period immediately following childbirth. Signs that one may be experiencing the baby blues include sudden mood swings, such as feeling very happy, then very sad, even crying without an obvious reason. Due to the sudden shift in many aspects of life and one's own hormones, this experience is normal and is not considered a psychiatric disorder.

Other symptoms include unhappiness, crying, anxiety, sleeplessness, loss of appetite, and irritability. Baby blues is a risk factor for postpartum depression.

The baby blues starts the first week after delivery. The peak of the emotional experience is often 3-5 days after delivery, and this period usually resolves by 10-12 days postpartum.

The baby blues occur in up to 85% of people following birth.

This period usually resolves on its own. If other resources are needed, these can include support groups, psychoeducation, and sleep hygiene techniques such as accepting help when offered in order to obtain more rest.

**Perinatal Depression**
Perinatal depression is depression that occurs anytime before, during, or up to 12 months after birth, with the postpartum period being an especially vulnerable period for many. Symptoms may begin gradually.

Perinatal depression most often begins in the first 3 months postpartum. Other moments that may trigger a depressive episode are after weaning baby or when the menstrual cycle resumes.

Risk factors for developing perinatal depression include a personal history of depression or postpartum depression, a family history of postpartum depression, fetal/newborn loss, lack of supportive resources, substance use, domestic violence, and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs).

Perinatal depression can last from 2 weeks up to a year or longer.

One in seven birthing people will experience perinatal depression.

Symptoms include changes in appetite, sleep, energy, motivation, concentration, and lack of self-care. One may experience negative thinking such as guilt, hopelessness, helplessness, and worthlessness. Some may also experience suicidal thoughts, psychotic symptoms, or thoughts of harming baby.

Treatment options include individual therapy, dyadic therapy for mother and baby, group therapy, and medication. Other ways to manage symptoms are to encourage self-care, engagement in social support, sleep hygiene and asking/accepting help from others during nighttime feedings.

**Perinatal Anxiety**
Perinatal anxiety disorders include a range of anxiety disorders, such as generalized anxiety, panic, and social anxiety, which are experienced during pregnancy and postpartum.

Perinatal anxiety starts immediately after delivery up to 6 weeks postpartum. Some may even begin experiencing symptoms during pregnancy, after weaning baby or when the menstrual cycle resumes.

Risk factors of perinatal anxiety disorders include a personal or family history of anxiety, lack of support, health challenges for mom or baby, prior pregnancy loss and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs).

Perinatal anxiety lasts from weeks to months, or even longer.

Generalized anxiety occurs in 6-8% of people in the first 6 months postpartum. Panic disorder occurs in 0.5-3% of people in the first 6-10 weeks postpartum.

Symptoms include fear and anxiety, panic attacks, shortness of breath, rapid pulse, dizziness, chest or stomach pains, body tension, sleep disturbances, sense of doom, and a fear of dying. Many people may experience intrusive thoughts, a fear of leaving the home, and repetitive checking behaviors.

Treatment options include individual therapy, dyadic therapy for mother and baby, and medication. Other ways to manage symptoms are to encourage self-care, exercise, nutritious eating, and engagement in social support. For some, behavioral exercises can be helpful to decrease nervous system dysregulation.

**Postpartum Psychosis**
Postpartum psychosis is a very rare and serious condition that includes the sudden onset of psychotic symptoms following childbirth. This disorder usually involves poor insight about the illness and symptoms, with people not being aware that anything is wrong, thus putting baby at risk. Psychotic symptoms include auditory hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, disorganization, and rarely visual hallucinations.

The onset of postpartum psychosis is usually between 24 hours up to 3 weeks following delivery. There is a higher risk if one is sleep deprived for more than 48 hours.

Risk factors include a current diagnosis of bipolar disorder (especially with associated medication discontinuation), history of psychosis, history of postpartum psychosis (80% will relapse), family history of psychotic illness, sleep deprivation, and prior pregnancy loss.

Postpartum psychosis usually lasts until it is treated.

Treatment of postpartum psychosis requires immediate psychiatric help and medication, with hospitalization usually being necessary. If one has a history of postpartum psychosis, preventative treatment is often needed in following pregnancies. Since sleep deprivation is a risk factor, it is important to encourage sleep hygiene (e.g., consistent sleep/wake times, help with feedings at night).

**Postpartum PTSD**
Postpartum PTSD includes distressing anxiety symptoms experienced after traumatic events. Symptoms of PTSD usually cluster around intrusion, avoidance, increased arousal or feeling "on edge", and a negative world view.

Onset of postpartum PTSD may be related to the labor and delivery process, a traumatic delivery, or poor birth outcome. Those with underlying PTSD diagnoses can also have symptoms that are worsened by a traumatic birth.

Postpartum PTSD can last one month or longer.

Postpartum PTSD occurs in 2-9% of people.

Symptoms include changes in cognition, mood, and arousal (feeling "on edge"), often with avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.

Treatment includes both individual and group therapy. Other ways to treat include encouraging self-care, exercise, healthy eating, accepting social support (such as support groups), and monitoring avoidance patterns. It is recommended for health care providers to maintain close follow up of those who have experienced traumatic births.

**Please contact UCI clinic if you have concerns you are experiencing any of these conditions. Please seek emergency services by calling 911 if you feel you may be in danger of hurting yourself or others so you can get timely care.**

Adapted from ACOG.

resources.title: Baby Blues vs. Postpartum Depression
resources.summary: Understanding the difference and when to seek help
resources.content:
Mood changes after birth are common, but some symptoms need attention. [ACOG recommends](https://www.acog.org/programs/perinatal-mental-health/patient-screening) screening all new parents for perinatal depression.

**Baby Blues (normal):**
- Affects up to 80% of new parents
- Starts within first few days after birth
- Lasts up to 2 weeks
- Symptoms: mood swings, crying, anxiety, irritability
- Resolves on its own

**[Postpartum Depression](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/postpartum-depression) (needs support):**
- Affects [1 in 7 new parents](https://www.acog.org/programs/perinatal-mental-health/patient-screening)
- Can start anytime in first year
- Lasts longer than 2 weeks
- Symptoms: persistent sadness, hopelessness, guilt
- Difficulty bonding with baby
- Changes in sleep or appetite
- Thoughts of harming yourself or baby

**Risk factors:**
- History of depression or anxiety
- Difficult pregnancy or birth
- Lack of support
- Major life stressors
- Previous postpartum depression

**Remember:**
- PPD is treatable
- It's not your fault
- Getting help is a sign of strength
- Treatment helps you and your baby

**Learn More:**
- [ACOG: Postpartum Depression](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/postpartum-depression)
- [Postpartum Support International](https://postpartum.net/)

resources.title: Self-Care for New Parents
resources.summary: Practical ways to take care of yourself
resources.content:
Taking care of yourself helps you take care of your baby.

**Sleep when you can:**
- Nap when baby naps
- Take shifts with partner
- Accept help with night feedings if possible

**Nourish your body:**
- Eat regular meals
- Keep easy snacks accessible
- Stay hydrated

**Connect with others:**
- Don't isolate yourself
- Join a new parent group
- Video chat with friends and family
- Accept visitors who offer to help

**Move your body (when cleared):**
- Short walks outside
- Gentle stretching
- Baby-wearing counts as exercise!

**Ask for help:**
- Be specific about what you need
- Let others do household tasks
- Use meal delivery services
- Don't aim for perfection

**Protect your mental health:**
- Limit social media
- Lower your expectations
- Celebrate small wins
- Talk about your feelings

resources.title: Getting Help for Emotional Struggles
resources.summary: Resources and next steps for support

image.alt: Group fist bump showing community support

resources.content:
If you're struggling, help is available. You don't have to face this alone.

**Talk to someone:**
- Your OB, midwife, or primary care provider
- Your baby's pediatrician
- A therapist specializing in perinatal mental health

**Crisis resources:**
- **[988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline](https://988lifeline.org/)**: Call or text 988 (24/7)
- **[Postpartum Support International](https://postpartum.net/get-help/)**: 1-800-944-4773 (call/text)
- **[National Maternal Mental Health Hotline](https://mchb.hrsa.gov/national-maternal-mental-health-hotline)**: 1-833-943-5746 (24/7)
- **Emergency**: Call 911

**What treatment looks like:**
- Therapy (talk therapy, CBT)
- [PSI Online Support Groups](https://postpartum.net/get-help/psi-online-support-groups/)
- Medication (many are safe while breastfeeding)
- Combination approaches

**What to say to your provider:**
- "I'm not feeling like myself"
- "I'm struggling more than I expected"
- "I'm having scary thoughts"
- "I need help"

**Remember:**
- Treatment works
- Most people improve significantly
- You deserve support
- Your baby needs you to be well

**Learn More:**
- [Postpartum Support International](https://postpartum.net/get-help/)
- [ACOG Mental Health Resources](https://www.acog.org/programs/perinatal-mental-health)

resources.title: Birth Trauma & Childbirth-Related PTSD
resources.summary: Understanding when a difficult birth experience affects your mental health
resources.content:
Sometimes birth doesn't go as planned, and the experience can leave a lasting emotional impact. Childbirth-related PTSD (CB-PTSD) is a real condition that affects roughly [5-11% of women](https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(23)00713-5/fulltext) after delivery. It's different from the baby blues or postpartum depression, and it often goes unrecognized.

**What is CB-PTSD?**
CB-PTSD occurs when the experience of labor and delivery is perceived as traumatic — whether due to medical complications, feeling out of control, fear for yourself or your baby, or feeling unheard by your care team. It can happen after any type of birth, including ones that others might consider "normal."

**Symptoms to watch for:**
- Flashbacks or intrusive memories of the birth
- Nightmares about the delivery
- Avoiding things that remind you of the birth (hospitals, birth stories, even your baby sometimes)
- Feeling emotionally numb or detached
- Being easily startled or on edge
- Difficulty bonding with your baby
- Guilt, anger, or shame about the birth experience

**Risk factors:**
- A birth that felt frightening or out of your control
- Emergency cesarean or unplanned interventions
- Premature birth or NICU stay
- Feeling unsupported or unheard during labor
- History of trauma, anxiety, or depression
- Previous difficult birth experience
- Prenatal distress or fear of childbirth

It's important to know that how you *experienced* the birth matters as much as what *medically* happened. Two people can have the same delivery and respond very differently — and both responses are valid.

**How is it different from PPD?**
- PPD involves persistent sadness, hopelessness, and difficulty functioning
- CB-PTSD is centered around the birth event itself — flashbacks, avoidance, hypervigilance
- They can overlap: [up to 90%](https://mghpsychnews.org/sharon-dekel-phd-focusing-on-the-psychological-consequences-of-traumatic-childbirth/) of women with CB-PTSD also have depressive symptoms
- Standard depression screening (like the EPDS) may not catch PTSD symptoms

**The good news — early help makes a difference:**
Because CB-PTSD has a clear onset (the birth itself), there's a window in the early postpartum period where support and intervention can be most effective. Talking about your birth experience soon after delivery — with a provider, counselor, or trained support person — can help.

**Effective treatments include:**
- Trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
- Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR)
- Birth story processing or debriefing with a trained professional
- Support groups with others who've had similar experiences
- Medication when symptoms are severe

**What you can do now:**
- If your birth felt traumatic, trust that feeling — it doesn't have to meet someone else's standard of "bad enough"
- Tell your provider: "My birth experience is still bothering me" or "I keep replaying my delivery"
- Ask for a referral to a therapist who specializes in perinatal trauma
- Know that healing is possible and you are not alone

**Crisis resources:**
- **[Postpartum Support International](https://postpartum.net/get-help/)**: 1-800-944-4773
- **[National Maternal Mental Health Hotline](https://mchb.hrsa.gov/national-maternal-mental-health-hotline)**: 1-833-943-5746 (24/7)
- **[988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline](https://988lifeline.org/)**: Call or text 988

**Learn More:**
- [Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health: CB-PTSD](https://policycentermmh.org/childbirth-related-post-traumatic-stress-disorder-cb-ptsd-a-critical-maternal-health-issue-that-must-be-addressed-systemically/)
- [ACOG: Screening for Perinatal Mental Health](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/clinical-practice-guideline/articles/2023/06/screening-and-diagnosis-of-mental-health-conditions-during-pregnancy-and-postpartum)
- [ACOG: Tokophobia and Fear of Childbirth](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/experts-and-stories/the-latest/tokophobia-what-to-know-about-this-severe-fear-of-pregnancy-and-childbirth)
- [Maternal Mental Health Screening Tools](https://policycentermmh.org/mmh-screening-tools/)

resources.title: Fear of Childbirth: When Anxiety Feels Overwhelming
resources.summary: Prenatal anxiety about labor and delivery is common and treatable
resources.content:
Feeling nervous about giving birth is completely normal. But for some people, that fear becomes intense enough to cause significant distress during pregnancy. You're not being dramatic — this is a recognized condition, and help is available.

**When is fear of childbirth more than normal nerves?**
- Constant worry or dread about labor and delivery
- Avoiding prenatal appointments or birth-related conversations
- Difficulty sleeping due to anxiety about the birth
- Requesting a cesarean solely out of fear
- Panic attacks when thinking about labor
- Considering not having children due to fear of childbirth

This level of fear is sometimes called [tokophobia](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/experts-and-stories/the-latest/tokophobia-what-to-know-about-this-severe-fear-of-pregnancy-and-childbirth), and it can occur whether this is your first pregnancy or you've given birth before.

**What can make it worse:**
- A previous traumatic birth or pregnancy loss
- History of sexual trauma or abuse
- Hearing frightening birth stories from others
- Anxiety or depression before or during pregnancy
- Feeling a loss of control or lack of information

**What actually helps:**

*Talk to your provider*
- Let them know about your fears early in pregnancy
- Ask questions about what to expect — the unknown is often scarier than reality
- Discuss your birth plan preferences so you feel more in control

*Therapy*
- Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is effective for fear of childbirth
- EMDR can help if the fear is linked to past trauma
- Even a few sessions can make a meaningful difference

*Education and preparation*
- Childbirth education classes that are evidence-based and realistic
- Tour the labor and delivery unit ahead of time
- Using this app's birth plan to think through your preferences
- Learning about pain management options so you know what's available

*Build your support team*
- A doula can provide continuous emotional and physical support
- Let your partner or support person know about your fears
- Your labor nurse will be your advocate during delivery

**What to say to your provider:**
- "I'm really scared about giving birth and it's affecting my daily life"
- "I had a bad experience before and I'm afraid it will happen again"
- "Can we talk about what I can expect so I feel more prepared?"

**Remember:**
- Fear of childbirth is not a character flaw
- Treatment during pregnancy can reduce fear and improve birth outcomes
- Having a plan and a supportive team makes a real difference
- Many people who felt terrified beforehand go on to have positive birth experiences

**Learn More:**
- [ACOG: Tokophobia — Fear of Pregnancy and Childbirth](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/experts-and-stories/the-latest/tokophobia-what-to-know-about-this-severe-fear-of-pregnancy-and-childbirth)
- [Postpartum Support International](https://postpartum.net/)
- [ACOG: Perinatal Mental Health Screening](https://www.acog.org/programs/perinatal-mental-health/implementing-perinatal-mental-health-screening)

resources.title: Getting Started with Breastfeeding
resources.summary: Tips for the first days and weeks
resources.content:
Breastfeeding is natural, but it takes practice for both you and baby. The [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/breastfeeding/php/about/index.html) and [AAP](https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/breastfeeding/) recommend exclusive breastfeeding for about the first 6 months.

**First hours:**
- Skin-to-skin contact helps initiate breastfeeding
- Baby may feed or just nuzzle at first
- Colostrum (first milk) is all baby needs initially

**First days:**
- Feed whenever baby shows hunger cues
- Expect 8-12 feedings per day
- Each session may last 10-45 minutes
- Both breasts don't need to be used each time

**Signs of good latch:**
- Wide open mouth with lips flanged out
- Chin touching breast
- Nose slightly away from breast
- No clicking sounds
- No pain after initial latch

**Signs baby is getting enough:**
- 6-8 wet diapers per day by day 4
- Yellow seedy stools
- Weight gain after initial loss
- Satisfied after feedings
- Audible swallowing

**Get help if:**
- Latching is painful
- Baby isn't gaining weight
- You have nipple damage
- Feeding takes over an hour every time

**Learn More:**
- [CDC Breastfeeding Guidelines](https://www.cdc.gov/breastfeeding/php/about/index.html)
- [La Leche League Support](https://llli.org/)

resources.title: Breastfeeding Nutrition and Safety
resources.summary: Recommendations for how to keep your body properly fueled for breastfeeding
resources.content:
Recommendations for how to keep your body properly fueled for breastfeeding.

**Diet:**
- Breastfeeding burns 450-500 calories a day
- Eat ~2500 calories if your weight is in normal range
- Eat fish 2-3 times per week but avoid those with high mercury
- Continue prenatal vitamins
- Hydrate with plenty of fluids

**Caffeine:**
- Moderate caffeine intake (200 mg per day) not likely to be harmful
- Check caffeine content of drinks and foods
- Newborns and preemies may be more sensitive

**Alcohol:**
- Wait at least two hours after a single drink to breastfeed
- No need to express and discard milk afterwards
- Alcohol will leave milk as it exits bloodstream
- More than 2 drinks per day may be harmful to baby

**Medications:**
- Most medications are safe
- Check LactMed and speak with your provider about prescription meds

**Smoking and Drug Use:**
- Quitting smoking is most ideal for your health and baby's health
- Breastfeeding is still better than formula feeding even if you smoke
- Do not smoke around baby
- Using illicit or non-prescribed drugs can be harmful to baby
- Marijuana should not be used while breastfeeding

**Learn More:**
- [ACOG: Breastfeeding Your Baby](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/breastfeeding-your-baby)
- [LactMed](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/)

resources.title: Common Breastfeeding Challenges
resources.summary: Many breastfeeding challenges have solutions. Don't give up!
resources.content:
Many breastfeeding challenges have solutions. Don't give up!

**Sore nipples:**
- Usually from shallow latch
- Apply expressed milk and let air dry
- Use lanolin cream
- Try different positions
- See a lactation consultant

**Engorgement:**
- Feed frequently
- Apply cold compresses between feedings
- Hand express for comfort if needed
- Wear supportive bra

**Low supply concerns:**
- Feed more frequently
- Ensure good latch
- Stay hydrated and nourished
- Consider pumping after feedings
- Most perceived low supply is actually normal

**Mastitis:**
- Flu-like symptoms with breast pain
- Red, hot area on breast
- Continue nursing to clear blockage
- Apply heat before feedings
- See provider—may need antibiotics

**Where to get help:**
- Hospital lactation consultants
- Private lactation consultants (IBCLC)
- [La Leche League](https://llli.org/) meetings
- Breastfeeding support groups

**Learn More:**
- [La Leche League: Find Local Support](https://lllusa.org/locator/)
- [La Leche League: Breastfeeding Info A-Z](https://llli.org/breastfeeding-info/)
- [CDC Breastfeeding FAQs](https://www.cdc.gov/breastfeeding/php/faq/faq.html)

resources.title: Formula Feeding Basics
resources.summary: Formula is a safe, nutritious option for feeding your baby
resources.content:
Formula is a safe, nutritious option for feeding your baby.

**Choosing formula:**
- Most babies do well on standard [cow's milk formula](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/formula-feeding/Pages/Choosing-an-Infant-Formula.aspx)
- Talk to your pediatrician before switching types
- Generic brands are nutritionally equivalent to name brands
- The [AAP recommends](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/formula-feeding/Pages/default.aspx) iron-fortified formula

**Preparation:**
- Follow package directions exactly
- Use the scoop that comes with the formula
- Use clean water (check if needs to be boiled)
- Prepare one bottle at a time when possible
- Never add extra water to formula

**Feeding:**
- Hold baby in semi-upright position
- Keep bottle tilted so nipple is full
- Let baby set the pace
- Burp during and after feeding
- Discard unfinished formula after 1 hour

**[Amount and frequency](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/formula-feeding/Pages/amount-and-schedule-of-formula-feedings.aspx):**
- Newborns: 1-3 oz every 2-3 hours
- Increases gradually over first months
- 24-32 oz total per day by one month
- Watch for hunger and fullness cues

**Remember:**
- Formula feeding is a valid choice
- Bonding happens with any feeding method
- Fed is best
